Las ecuaciones de primer y segundo grado: First- and second-degree equations are already dealt with; so are the intervals of the real line. This topic brings them together: you swap the $=$ for a $<$ and the answer stops being a number and becomes an interval. The technique for isolating the unknown is the same, with a single new rule, and the quadratic's parabola turns up again to decide where an expression is positive.
Una <strong>inecuación</strong> es como: An inequality is like an equation but with an inequality sign instead of the equals sign. And that changes the nature of the answer: it is no longer a number, it is a whole stretch of the line.

El mundo real casi nunca dice «exactamen: The real world almost never says “exactly”; it says “at most” and “at least”. The budget cannot go above so much, the beam has to take at least so much, the temperature must stay between two values. That is why inequalities describe reality better than equations, and why the set of solutions is not a point but a region. That region has a name and a topic of its own: it is called the feasible region and you will meet it in linear programming.
Los signos $<$ y $>$ los introdujo el in: The signs $<$ and $>$ were introduced by the Englishman Thomas Harriot, and published in 1631, ten years after his death. The $\le$ took two more centuries to become general. That such simple symbols took so long to settle gives an idea of how slowly notation moves: for generations, every mathematician wrote in their own way and reading a foreign colleague was half a translation job.
